text.en: The Rav reads the opening bracha of the Avos as an act of identifying with the Avos who instituted tefillah, so that tefillah begins by joining oneself to them.
Davening with kavanah means meeting the heart that the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah put into the nusach with our own heart, to the degree of our kavanah.
The Rav points out that the Ramban's view is in practice the stricter one, since in golus, before Mashiach, the whole world is in a time of trouble.
The twelve middle brachos parallel the twelve shevatim, the branches of the tree; on Shabbos one rises above the branches to the trunk, the Avos, like Yerushalayim which belongs to all the tribes.
The word 'leyom' teaches that on Shabbos no one sings for the day; the day itself sings, unlike Sunday, for which there is no 'song of the first day'.

Every seventh sings: Eretz Yisrael, the seventh land, is called Zimras HaAretz; the Kinneres, the seventh sea, takes its name from the kinor; and David HaMelech, the seventh of the ushpizin, is the singer of Israel.
Bereishis counts as the first of the ten utterances because it created speech itself, before any utterance existed, and like every beginning it contains all that follows.

Menuchah is not merely the absence of creating; the fact that Hashem rested was itself a creation, the satisfaction of lacking nothing, and that is why people sing 'Shabbos' when dancing before a chassan and kallah even on a weekday.
Pesukei D'zimra comes from the word for pruning, as in cutting the branches of a vineyard: the verses cut away the accusers who block the tefillos.
Saying David's Tehillim is like carrying a letter stamped by the king's minister: the guards must let it through, and once the way is cleared, one's own tefillos rise after it.
On weekdays the Levi'im sang for the day, but on Shabbos the day itself sings, because Shabbos is the completion of the harp's seven strings.
The song of Shabbos does not mention Shabbos because it sings of history's harmony and its purpose, the day that is entirely Shabbos, of which the weekly Shabbos is a miniature.
The Rav reads the three 'havu' and seven 'kol' of Mizmor LeDavid as the ten utterances of creation: three upper levels beyond time and seven that crystallized into the seven days.
Music, a painting and a marriage all depend on the same thing, a true match between their parts; the music at a chasunah and the badchan's rhymes express the match of the couple.
Kabbalas Shabbos opens with song because on the seventh day the harp of seven notes is complete; only then is there harmony and yichud in the world.
Not saying the weekday brachos on Shabbos loses nothing: their blessing comes through the eighteen names in Mizmor LeDavid, and through resting from one's mundane needs.
The second day of creation lacks 'ki tov' because plurality, separation and dispute entered creation then, the opposite of Shabbos, the domain of the One.
'Kol Hashem al hamayim', the first voice of the psalm, is the border officer's first question as one enters Shabbos: did you go to the mikvah?
The Rav reads 'bnei eilim' as the strong and respected people themselves, who are called upon to give their own power and prowess back to Hashem.
The 'kol Hashem' of the psalm is the Ten Utterances of creation, which still live inside every natural force, so the destructive might of the ocean is Hashem concealing Himself in the water.
Recognizing that an enemy's power is really Hashem's is itself a sweetening of judgment (hamtakas hadinim), after which the din has no hold over the person.

The cedars of the psalm are the great powers that, like tall trees in a forest, block a person's view of heaven; the Rav applies this to communist Russia, where belief was forbidden and which collapsed overnight.
Looking up to the sky for Hashem follows a human instinct that power comes from above, though Hashem has no place; still, seeing the sky gives emunah and kavanah.
The 39 melachos forbidden on Shabbos are the 39 curses given after the sin of the Eitz HaDaas, so Shabbos, a day of blessing, has no place for them.
Shabbos could not wait the forty-nine days of the long Exodus until Matan Torah, so it was already given at Marah.
The different reasons for Shabbos in the two luchos match the people's level: prophets see the Creator in nature itself, while after the golden calf they needed the remembered miracles of Egypt.
The ten plagues repeat the ten utterances of creation in reverse: the first utterance corresponds to the last plague, the firstborn, and 'let there be light' to the ninth plague, darkness.
Denial of the Creator is not an intellectual position but a refusal: the heretic does not believe his own house built itself, yet claims the world did, because admitting the truth would bind him.
An event seen by millions cannot be invented, so the Exodus entered history and was handed down from generation to generation, a tradition no other nation has.

The thirty-nine melachos of Shabbos correspond to the curses that Adam, Chavah, the earth and the serpent received after the sin, so refraining from them on Shabbos is a return to a state of pure blessing.
The amount of melachah permitted on a day is the inverse of the blessing it holds: Shabbos none, Yom Tov somewhat more, Chol Hamoed more, Rosh Chodesh more still.
Moshe's argument to Pharaoh that rested workers produce more is what modern scientists call the law of diminishing returns, yet the Torah's Shabbos is the opposite of such a practical day off.
Moshe's joy in 'Yismach Moshe b'matnas chelko' is that the day he had chosen in Egypt turned out to be the very day Hashem gave as Shabbos.
Food prepared with words of tefillah carries them: the fish over which Nishmas was said had Nishmas in it, which is the meaning of 'echol b'simchah' after 'Nishmas kol chai' in Menuchah v'Simchah.
Some have a Shabbosdik kugel, a kugel infused with Shabbos, and others a kugeldik Shabbos, a Shabbos that amounts to another piece of kugel.

The Rav reads the two kiddush formulas as two kinds of holiness: Shabbos comes down as Hashem's own gift, while Yom Tov's holiness is drawn from below by the Jews, and grows with how well each one prepared.
Even though Shabbos is a gift that does not depend on preparation, the receiver must be a clean vessel; the gift is the same, but in a dirty cup it has no taste.
What a person has in mind during the week is what he brings into Shabbos: the storekeeper thought of kiddush while selling and his kiddush burned, while the scholar thought of the women at kiddush.
Following the Tikkunei Zohar that 'Bereishis' holds the letters of 'yarei Shabbos', the Rav says one must approach Shabbos with fear and shame, asking whether he is a clean vessel for it.
When one prepares properly, even the physical things of Shabbos carry its holiness, as the Karliner chassid asked Hashem to give Shabbos to his wine and his fish.
The Rav reads 'Lev tahor' in Tehillim as hinting at tevilah, so that immersing before Shabbos helps one attain a pure heart.
A mikveh becomes kosher by touching and joining the rainwater from heaven; in the same way, before Shabbos a Jew purifies himself by connecting to tzaddikim and their sefarim.
Since Shabbos is a gift and a giver gives generously, Hashem gave not only Shabbos but also the path to it, erev Shabbos; one cannot fall into Shabbos unprepared but must walk the path.
The passuk ties 'Hashem gave you Shabbos' to the double bread of the sixth day, showing that Friday itself is part of the gift, the road by which one enters Shabbos.
Erev Shabbos is a form of Yom Kippur, as the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's answer to the Chida shows: the Yom Kippur-like asking of forgiveness on erev Shabbos is what made his name great in heaven.
A 'shomer Shabbos' is literally one who waits for Shabbos, as 'shamar' is used for Yaakov awaiting the fulfillment of Yosef's dreams.
The seven days of the week correspond to the ushpizin; Friday is Yosef HaTzaddik, who is holiness, so the preparation for Shabbos must be with holiness, while Shabbos is Dovid.

Following the Chasam Sofer, 'lo seva'aru esh... b'yom haShabbos' is read as: do not wait until Shabbos to kindle the fire; kindle it at the start of the week in learning and davening, so that on Shabbos the fire of Shabbos flares up.

Because good joins with good while evil does not join with evil ('yispardu kol po'alei aven'), a gathering of Jews combines only their good points, like many small candles that together become one great flame.

The seven notes of music correspond to the seven days and middos; only when Shabbos, the seventh, arrives is the 'piano' complete, which is why Psalm 29 with its seven 'kol Hashem' is the seventh chapter of Kabbalas Shabbos, and only after it is Lecha Dodi sung.

Unlike the weekday psalms, which the Levi'im sang, 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' means that the Shabbos day itself sings, so the Jew's singing on Shabbos is joining in harmony with the day's own song.
At shalosh seudos 'da hi seudasa' is said only after eating a little and right before singing, because the real seudah of shalosh seudos is the singing, not the herring.

The tzaddik is compared to both the date palm and the cedar: the palm puts its strength into fruit and so does not grow tall, the cedar grows tall but bears no fruit, and the tzaddik has both qualities.
Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested from it on Shabbos, a person who strives higher rests on Shabbos from ordinary speech as well, not only from work.
A great spiritual level cannot be made an obligation; this is why tefillas chatzos is a takanah rather than a chiyuv.
The Rav reads 'bechorish' in the passuk about resting as related to cheresh, silence: on Shabbos a person is quiet.
Shabbos is compared to the private talk of two close friends that others are not meant to hear, a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel alone.
The afternoon, which during the week carries harsh judgment at mincha, is on Shabbos the peak of the day and a time of great ratzon.
'Bnei Heichala' are the children of the King's palace whom the King invites to come and eat together with Him.

The 'will of wills' is read on two levels: plainly, the et ratzon of mincha within the favor of all Shabbos; more deeply, the will Hashem had before creation, which a Jew can echo by willing to become a new person.
Since the world was created on Sunday, Shabbos afternoon before motzaei Shabbos is like the time before the first day, which is why shalosh seudos is above time.
Just as the aron in the Kodesh HaKodashim took up no space, shalosh seudos is not bound by time; created limits of place and time do not apply where there is a revelation of heaven.
The three Avos received the land in different ways, and only Yaakov's promise has no borders; shalosh seudos is Yaakov's portion, so the clock announcing the end of Shabbos has no hold on it.
Because kiddush is testimony and a rasha is an invalid witness, teshuvah before kiddush is what qualifies a person to testify to creation.

The Rav joins Rashi's point that the future Mikdash will come down built by Hashem with the idea that all melacha stems from sin, so that the Mishkan's construction is itself a product of sin and cannot override Shabbos.
The word 'kallah' is read as 'kolel', all-inclusive, and the bond of each kallah to Knesses Yisrael is modeled on Chavah, built from Adam's own body: the partner is a piece of the person himself.
The Mikdash is the Shabbos of place and Shabbos the Mikdash of time; since time stands above place, the 'ach' limiting Shabbos refers to the smaller Shabbos, the Mishkan, yielding to the greater one.

Dovid HaMelech did not build the Mikdash because he himself was the seventh, the embodiment of Shabbos; building a Mikdash of place would have been a lessening for one who already carried the Mikdash of Shabbos in his heart.
'Ledorosam' read as 'ledirosam' means both that each Jew becomes a dwelling for Shabbos and that a home steeped in Shabbos is a guarantee that the coming generations will remain Jews.
The rising kedushah of Shabbos explains the shrinking kiddush: Friday night needs the full blessing, the morning only wine, and at Shalosh Seudos the eating itself sanctifies Shabbos.

The Gemara's 'go and make it known' is explained through a chasan's diamond: a gift whose worth the recipient cannot see must be explained, so Hashem told Klal Yisroel that Shabbos is not 'just a mitzvah' but a personal token of His bond with them.
The prohibition 'lo s'vaaru esh... b'yom haShabbos' is read as: the fire of Shabbos cannot be lit once Shabbos arrives; it must be kindled already during the week.
The six weekdays correspond to six sefiros; erev Shabbos is Yosef and middas hayesod, so 'v'hayah bayom hashishi v'heichinu' points to kedushas habris as the preparation for Shabbos.
A tzaddik explains Nishmas: until Nishmas one davens with body and soul, but from Nishmas on with the soul alone, as if the body did not exist.
Since Hashem's 'work' in creation was speech, His resting on the seventh day means that a Jew guards Shabbos above all in his speech.
The food of Shabbos is a continuation of the mann: one who eats the Shabbos cholent eats, as it were, mann, which is why tzaddikim gave Shabbos kugel as a remedy.
The three parts of Shabbos parallel the stages of a marriage: Friday night is kiddushin, Shabbos morning is nisuin, and Shabbos mincha is yichud, when one says 'Atah Echad'.
The Shabbos seudah is even greater than the Shabbos Amidah; the tefillah is the preparation for the seudah.
The mincha Amidah of Shabbos has no pesukim because it is above pesukim, like the tip of the yud, and so shalosh seudos is a short, simple meal of challah and herring.
What is beyond place is beyond time: the manna in the Kodesh Hakodashim was not 'left over till morning', and shalosh seudos has no time until bentching.
No tevilah is required before Shabbos mincha because the time itself is the mikveh, as Yom Kippur is, and Jews gathered together are a mikveh.
Moshe Rabbeinu passed away at Shabbos mincha, rising to a place beyond human measure, and therefore no one knows his burial place.
Shabbos morning is felt less than Friday night precisely because its kedushah is higher, and mincha even more so.
The Rav reads 'Zachor es yom haShabbos l'kadsho' as an instruction to make a Shabbos worth remembering: a Shabbos of such davening, learning and singing that one remembers it long afterwards.
The lechem hapanim is not a korban placed on a vessel but part of the Table itself, which explains both why its 'tamid' is written in Parshas Terumah and why its baking does not override Shabbos.
The kohanim eating the lechem hapanim on Shabbos expresses that on Shabbos a Jew himself becomes the Mishkan, taking a piece of the Mishkan into himself.
Achashverosh's 'k'tov lev hamelech bayayin' on the seventh day shows a Shabbos without preparation: since by mazal Shabbos is a heavy day for him, he needed wine to cheer himself up.
The seventh officer, Memuchan, whose name the Gemara reads as 'heichinu', corresponds to Shabbos, because the whole character of Shabbos is that it cannot be had without preparation.
Purim is like an anesthetic before surgery: its revelation is too great for a person to bear consciously, so one drinks until 'lo yada'.
Sin is a 'passing of Moshe' within a person, but teshuvah turns it into a 'birth of Moshe' on a higher level, as Moshe Rabbeinu passed away and was born in Adar.
